one_child_she_version.text: Last time: a cold, wet fox tapped at the last lit window in Candlemere, with news that the beacon on Wardlow had gone out.
In the morning, Candlemere was grey. No chimney smoked, not one lamp flickered, and every window on the lane looked as sleepy as a yawn. Somebody had to carry Grandma's flame to Wardlow, and soon.
"Let's ask the neighbors," said Robin. "A grown-up will go."
Grandma stood in the doorway, where she could see the whole lane. "Every door," she said. "And stay where I can see you."
So off went Robin down the lane, with Ember trotting close beside, her tail held high, because it was Tuesday.
The baker opened the bakehouse door in a puff of flour. "Someone should," he said. "But not I. The bread won't bake itself."
"Good morning," said Ember, very politely.
But all the baker heard was *yip, yip*. "Noisy fox," he said, not unkindly, and shut the door.
Ember sniffed. Nobody had ever called her noisy before.
Next door, the miller came out slowly, rubbing his knees. "Not I," he said. "These old knees won't climb Wardlow."
Then Reeve Osric hurried past with his arms full of tally-sticks. "Yes, yes," he said. "We'll see to it tomorrow."
"How many tomorrows has that been?" whispered Robin.
"One, two, three, four, lots," whispered Ember.
And so it went, all along the lane. Everybody agreed that someone should go. But nobody was willing to be the one. At every door the answer was the same: "Not I."
Then Will, the baker's boy, came pelting round the corner. "I'll go right now," he shouted, "and I dare anybody to stop me!" Off he ran into the old holloway, with no light at all.
The holloway was a sunken lane under the trees, dark even at noon.
Robin wanted to dare the dark too, and run in after him. But part of her wanted to run home and hide. So Robin stood still, which was the hardest thing of all.
*Splosh!* Before anyone could count to twenty, Will came back out of the dark, muddy from his boots to his ears, and a little sheepish.
"There's a puddle," said Will, "in the dark."
Nobody laughed. Ember went and stood right next to the muddy boy, so Will wouldn't be muddy all on his own. Robin wiped the worst of the mud off with a sleeve.
By the Moot Hall door sat old Hild the wick-woman, with her tray of needles, thread and lamp-wicks. Her donkey, Dun, dozed at her side. On the door behind her hung an old notice.
Robin read it out loud: "Beacon Night. All welcome. Bring one stick."
Old Brock lay on the step, the way the old dog always did, and did not get up for anyone. Robin stopped to pat him anyway.
"Good morning," said Ember.
"Good morning, fox," said Hild, as if foxes wished her good morning every day of the week.
Robin stared. The wick-woman could understand Ember too!
Then Hild beckoned Robin close, while Ember tried to count the wicks and got as far as lots.
Hild looked at Robin for a long, quiet moment. "How big must a person be to carry a lantern?" asked Hild.
Robin opened her mouth, and shut it again. Hild only waited, the way old folk wait for a kettle to sing.
Then Hild gave Robin something from her tray that wasn't on it at all: a question, to keep in a pocket. "For when I'm not there," she said. "There will be more, one day."
To Robin: "What's the brave thing, and what's the silly thing?"
Last of all, Hild put a little brass bell into Robin's hand. "Ring it if you ever lose your way," she said. "Stand still, ring, and call."
Then Hild went back to her wicks, as if nothing much had happened at all.
Robin looked at the bell, and then at Will, muddy and bedraggled on the step. Then out went the bell, and a hand too. "You carry the bell."

Will took the bell, and the hand. *Ting-a-ling!* Not one bit sheepish now, Will rang it all the way back up the lane, very loudly and very proudly. It was the only bright sound in the whole grey lane, and here and there a curtain twitched.
Ember trotted beside him with her ears folded flat, looking pained.
At the cottage gate, Will gave the bell back with a grin. "When the beacon's lit again," he said, "I'll carry a stick up Wardlow myself."
Back by the fire, Grandma listened to all of it.

Robin looked into the fire, thinking about the long road and the dark, and her tummy went wobbly. Nobody on the whole lane had been willing. Then Robin stood up, held an invisible lantern up high, and took one step forward.
"I'll help," she said. "With a proper light, and all of us together. Lantern up!"
A hush fell over the cottage. Then the fire gave a small pop, as if it agreed.
Robin packed the little backpack, and in went the apples, one at a time.
"One, two, three, four, lots," said Ember helpfully.
"Seven," said Robin.
"And I shall come too," said Ember. "Somebody has to know the way, and foxes are extremely good at roads."
Ember tried to help with the boots too, and got her nose stuck in one.
Grandma laughed, and pulled the boot off Ember's nose. "Nobody's too small to carry a light," she said. "But nobody carries it alone."

That night the little brass bell sat on the mantel, next to the note from home. Ember slept curled on the quilt like a warm red scarf, and the apples slept in the backpack. Robin fell asleep last. Hild's question was still there, the way a smooth stone stays in your pocket.
